title.en: History: State and Society in Medieval India

text.en: Asha visited a fort and saw old temples nearby. "Who built these?" she asked.

Medieval India saw many kingdoms. In the north, the Delhi Sultanate was ruled by dynasties such as the Slaves, Khaljis and Tughlaqs. In the south, the Cholas, Pandyas and later Vijayanagar ruled, and the Cholas built the Brihadeeswarar temple at Thanjavur.
The Mughal empire was founded by Babur in 1526, and Akbar, Shah Jahan and others ruled. Land revenue and an administrative system supported the state. The Bhakti and Sufi movements promoted unity and devotion.
Art and architecture flourished, with forts, mosques, temples and the Taj Mahal. Trade connected India to many lands.

In the south, the Cholas, Pandyas and later Vijayanagar ruled, and the Cholas built the Brihadeeswarar temple at Thanjavur.
The Mughal empire was founded by Babur in 1526, and Akbar, Shah Jahan and others ruled.
Land revenue and an administrative system supported the state.
The Bhakti and Sufi movements promoted unity and devotion.
Art and architecture flourished, with forts, mosques, temples and the Taj Mahal.
Trade connected India to many lands.
Medieval India stretched roughly from the eighth to the seventeenth century CE, witnessing the rise of mighty regional and pan-Indian kingdoms, flourishing trade and rich cultural synthesis.
In South India, the Imperial Cholas under Rajaraja Chola I and Rajendra Chola I built a powerful navy, expanded trade across Southeast Asia, and erected the Brihadeeswarar Temple at Thanjavur.
Chola administration was famous for autonomous village assemblies—Ur and Sabha—that managed irrigation tanks, land records and local justice.
In North India, the Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526) spanned five dynasties: Slave, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi, introducing the iqta system of land-revenue assignments.
In 1336, Harihara and Bukka founded the Vijayanagara Empire on the banks of the Tungabhadra, reaching its golden age under Krishnadevaraya, patron of Telugu, Sanskrit and Tamil arts.
Alongside Vijayanagara rose the Bahmani Kingdom in the Deccan, later dividing into five Deccan Sultanates that blended Persian and Indian architectural styles.

In 1526, Babur won the First Battle of Panipat and founded the Mughal Empire. Akbar consolidated the empire through the mansabdari system, Todar Mal's land-revenue survey and Sulh-i-Kul (peace with all).
Under Shah Jahan, Mughal architecture peaked with the Taj Mahal and Red Fort, while in western India Chhatrapati Shivaji built the Maratha state with an efficient Ashtapradhan council.
Across medieval India, agriculture remained the backbone of the economy. Rulers and communities expanded tanks, wells, Persian wheels and canals to irrigate paddy, wheat, cotton and indigo.
India was a workshop of the world for fine cotton textiles, silk, spices, steel and metalwork. Guilds like Manigramam and Ayyavole in South India organised vast overland and maritime trade.
Thriving ports like Calicut, Nagapattinam, Masulipatnam and Surat connected India with Arabia, East Africa, China and Southeast Asia, earning huge inflows of gold and silver.

text.en: In religion and culture, the Bhakti movement—sparked early in Tamil Nadu by the Nayanmars (Shaiva) and Alvars (Vaishnava)—preached loving devotion in everyday local languages.

board.text: Bhakti movement: Nayanmars & Alvars in TN

text.en: Later Bhakti saints across India—Kabir, Guru Nanak, Mirabai, Basavanna, Tukaram and Chaitanya—challenged caste rigidity and empty ritual, celebrating human equality.
Parallel to Bhakti, Sufi saints like Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti and Nizamuddin Auliya emphasised love, music, charity and harmony across communities.
Medieval art and architecture fused Indian and Persian traditions into Indo-Islamic domes, arches and gardens, alongside soaring Dravidian gopurams and bronze Nataraja sculptures.

board.text: Dravidian temples, Chola bronzes & Indo-Islamic art

text.en: Literature blossomed in Tamil, Sanskrit, Persian, Hindi, Telugu, Kannada, Marathi and Urdu—from Kamban's Ramavataram to Abul Fazl's Akbarnama.
Meanwhile, Vasco da Gama's arrival at Calicut in 1498 opened direct sea routes from Europe, bringing Portuguese, Dutch, French and English trading companies to Indian shores.
At first Europeans traded peacefully under Indian rulers' permission, building coastal factories, before gradually competing for political control as the Mughal Empire weakened after 1707.

text.en: Society remained stratified by caste and gender, yet vibrant towns, artisan workshops, devotional songs and temple festivals fostered rich everyday community life.
Notice how South and North India were deeply linked: Bhakti ideas travelled north from Tamil Nadu, while Persian administration, architecture and trade goods flowed south.
To revise medieval India cleanly, track four pillars: Political dynasties, Agrarian & guild trade, Bhakti & Sufi synthesis, and Temple/Indo-Islamic architecture.
Medieval India left behind an enduring legacy of pluralistic culture, world-renowned craftsmanship, regional languages and magnificent monuments.

problem.en: How did the Bhakti and Sufi movements help bridge social divisions in medieval India?

text.en: Look at the language they used.

why.en: Instead of restricting ideas to Sanskrit or Arabic, saints composed poems and songs in Tamil, Hindi, Marathi, Punjabi and Kannada so ordinary people could participate.

text.en: Look at their social message.

why.en: Saints like Kabir, Guru Nanak, Basavanna and the Alvars/Nayanmars taught that sincere devotion mattered more than caste birth or wealth.

text.en: Note the lasting effect.

why.en: They enriched regional languages and promoted mutual respect across communities.
